title: Despite new powers, industry minister hasn't forced telecoms to remove Huawei equipment

blocks.text: Politics·New

Despite legislating new powers last spring to force telecommunications companies to remove products considered a security risk, the minister of industry hasn't used them — and the Conservative Opposition is asking why.
Chinese tech giant convicted in U.S. this week of conspiring to steal trade secrets

Bill C-8 received royal assent in June, enabling the federal government to restrict or ban equipment or services that could put Canada's telecommunications system at risk of "interference, manipulation, disruption or degradation"
Although no companies were named in the bill, it was a successor to a Trudeau-era bill targeting Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE.
On Tuesday, Huawei was convicted of 10 U.S. charges, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets.

blocks.text: For years, Huawei hasn't been allowed to sell equipment to U.S. telecommunications carriers due to security concerns. All of Canada's Five Eyes allies have banned Huawei's 5G equipment.
While Canada has committed to cracking down on companies still using the equipment, it hasn't used its enforcement mechanisms to do so.

A 2022 policy statement named Huawei and ZTE as at risk of being "compelled to comply with extrajudicial directions from foreign governments." The statement includes deadlines to stop using — and rip out — the equipment.
The next deadline — Dec. 31, 2027 — prohibits all 4G equipment and managed services from Huawei and ZTE. The deadline to remove 5G equipment was in 2024.
CBC News reported in 2024 that all major telecommunications companies except Telus Corp. were co-operating with the policy directive.

Telus did not respond to a request for comment about its compliance with the policy. But the company told the Globe and Mail last year that it doesn't consider its equipment subject to the 2024 deadline.
Conservatives point to relations with China
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly now has the ability to compel any companies not in compliance to remove the gear.

"It was well understood at the time that Huawei and ZTE were indeed high-risk firms. And the minister has not exercised that power yet," said Conservative industry critic Adam Chambers in an interview on Tuesday.

"The government has now seemingly had a change of position with respect to engagement on Beijing, and I think Canadians deserve to know if that is the reason for which the minister has not yet used that power."

U.S. prosecutors had originally also brought criminal charges against Huawei's chief financial officer, Meng Wanzhou, accusing her of misleading HSBC bank about the company's business dealings in Iran.
Meng was arrested in Canada in 2018, which led to a diplomatic crisis involving the U.S., Canada and China.
The Huawei executive ultimately was allowed to return to China in 2021 in a prisoner swap that freed two Canadians held by China. As part of the deal, the U.S. dropped its case against Meng.

blocks.text: The company was acquitted on two additional counts, including the most serious: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy.
In a statement posted online, Huawei said the acquittal on the racketeering charge "confirms these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years."
Joly's department said that the government of Canada is "fully committed to protecting the security and reliability of Canadian networks."
"Orders under the Telecommunications Act will be made in due course, in consultation with affected parties," reads a statement from Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED).
Huawei Technologies is one of the biggest suppliers of gear for telecommunications networks in the world. U.S. authorities have long claimed the company poses national security risks.
